strengths: First comprehensive study of MLLM robustness to misleading visualizations, spanning 18 MLLMs (2B to 38B, open and commercial) and 17 misleader types, combining a well-motivated set of existing datasets (CALVI, CHARTOM, VLAT) with a new 42-instance real-world dataset derived from an established misleader taxonomy (Lo et al. 2022).

Three complementary experiments (QA accuracy, Likert-scale consistency, and correction methods) provide converging evidence for the central claim that MLLMs are vulnerable to misleading visualizations, with accuracy dropping to near-random levels on misleading charts versus strong performance on ChartQA.

Useful comparison to human performance on the same benchmarks (CALVI, CHARTOM), revealing interesting and non-trivial divergences between which misleaders fool humans vs. MLLMs (e.g., area encoding vs. dual axis), which is a genuinely novel and informative finding.

The correction-method experiments are methodically designed with a clear dual objective (improve misleading accuracy without hurting non-misleading accuracy), appropriate significance testing (McNemar test), and insightful follow-up analysis diagnosing *why* methods succeed or fail (e.g., the table-extraction consistency analysis on CHARTOM pairs showing only 7% perfect matches between misleading/non-misleading table extractions).

Practical, actionable findings: table-based QA and redrawing are shown to be effective with quantified trade-offs, and negative results (axes-only, warnings) are reported honestly and analyzed rather than omitted.

The paper is clearly written, well-organized, and includes thorough documentation of datasets, misleader definitions, and implementation details, supporting reproducibility, with code/data release promised.
weaknesses: The misleading and non-misleading datasets are small (n=143 and n=124 respectively), and per-misleader breakdowns are based on very small counts (several categories have n=1 or n=3), making claims about relative difficulty of specific misleader types (e.g., overplotting, missing data at exactly 0%) statistically fragile and likely not generalizable.

Correction methods are evaluated on only 3 mid-sized open-weight models (Qwen2VL-7B, Ovis1.6-9B, InternVL2.5-8B) out of the 18 studied in Experiment 1, and specifically models that started below the random baseline; it is unclear whether the correction methods generalize to larger or commercial models, or to models that already performed reasonably (e.g., GPT4o, Gemini-1.5-pro), limiting the generality of the correction-method conclusions.

Table-based QA, the most effective method, essentially discards the original visual input and reframes the task as text-only table QA; while practically useful, this somewhat sidesteps rather than solves the underlying visual misinterpretation problem, and its effectiveness is arguably unsurprising given it removes the misleading stimulus itself.

The new real-world MCQ dataset's annotation process (manual question/answer creation) is not validated with inter-annotator agreement or human calibration, raising reproducibility/validity questions about difficulty and answer correctness for this subset.

Known dataset imbalance (truncated/inverted axes dominate) is acknowledged as a limitation but not mitigated, which weakens the robustness of misleader-type-specific conclusions drawn throughout the results section.

Some interpretive claims (e.g., that real-world subset gains stem from parametric knowledge beyond 2022) are plausible but not directly tested/verified (e.g., no ablation removing date-sensitive knowledge or checking date cutoffs against specific instances).

strengths: Addresses a timely and societally important problem: the vulnerability of MLLMs to misleading data visualizations, which is directly relevant to disinformation and to the growing use of MLLMs as chart-understanding assistants.

Comprehensive empirical scope: 18 MLLMs (open-weight and commercial, ranging 2B-38B params, plus chart-specialized models) are evaluated across three complementary experiments (accuracy, Likert-scale consistency, and correction methods), providing a richer picture than prior single-model or narrow studies.

The headline finding that MLLM accuracy on misleading visualizations collapses to chance level is a striking and well-supported result, with clear comparison against ChartQA performance and against human baselines from CALVI/CHARTOM.

The paper contributes a new dataset of 42 real-world misleading visualizations with manually created MCQs, complementing existing synthetic benchmarks (CALVI, CHARTOM) and enabling assessment of conflicts with parametric knowledge.

The six proposed inference-time correction methods are a genuine novel contribution (first of their kind for this problem), and the finding that table-based QA and redrawing are effective while other approaches (warnings, axis/table augmentation) are not, is a useful, nuanced result with clear mechanistic explanation (removal vs. supplementation of the misleading image).
Appropriate use of statistical testing (McNemar's test, paired t-test) to validate claimed improvements and inconsistencies, rather than relying on point-estimate differences alone.

Thoughtful discussion of table-extraction quality as the bottleneck for the two effective correction methods, including a clever diagnostic using CHARTOM's misleading/non-misleading pairs of the same underlying data to quantify extraction inconsistency.

Honest limitations section (map redrawing unsupported, chart-type assumed known, dataset misleader-type imbalance) and clear positioning against very recent concurrent work in the related work section.
weaknesses: Dataset sizes are quite small overall (143 misleading, 124 non-misleading instances) and extremely small per misleader category in several cases (n=1 for overplotting, missing data, inappropriate pie-chart use; n=3 for several others), making per-misleader accuracy claims in Figure 5 and related discussion statistically fragile.

Experiment 3 (correction methods) is evaluated on only 3 mid-sized open-weight MLLMs (Qwen2VL-7B, Ovis1.6-9B, InternVL2.5-8B), chosen because they fell below the random baseline in Experiment 1; it remains unclear whether the correction methods generalize to the larger/commercial models (GPT4o, Gemini-1.5-pro, InternVL2.5-38B) that already perform comparatively better, limiting the generality of the correction-method conclusions.

The misleader-warning correction method assumes oracle knowledge of the specific misleader present, which the authors themselves acknowledge makes its reported performance an unrealistic upper bound; this weakens the practical takeaway of that comparison and by extension slightly weakens the overall claim that only two of six methods 'work,' since the warning method was tested under favorable, unrealistic conditions while still underperforming.

The manually created MCQs for the new real-world misleading-visualization subset lack reported inter-annotator agreement or validation, raising reproducibility/quality concerns for this specific contributed resource.

The correction methods themselves (prompted axis/table extraction, table-based QA, code-generated redrawing) are technically straightforward engineering pipelines built from off-the-shelf components (Qwen2.5-7B, Matplotlib); the contribution is more empirical/evaluative than methodologically novel, which is appropriate framing but limits the technical depth of the contribution.

Table-based QA's accuracy gains come with a non-trivial accuracy cost on non-misleading visualizations for some models (up to 8.5pp drop), and the paper does not propose or evaluate a mechanism (e.g., misleader detection gating) to realize the suggested 'selective application' idea, leaving the main practical trade-off unresolved beyond a suggestion for future work.

The claims of being 'first' (first inference-time correction methods, first comprehensive study) are only partially distinguished from several concurrent 2025 papers cited in related work (Bendeck & Stasko; Chen et al.; Pandey & Ottley), and the differentiation offered (real-world data, correction methods) is reasonable but somewhat narrow given how close in time these works are.

strengths: Addresses a timely and societally relevant vulnerability (misleading visualizations) in MLLM-based chart understanding that has been largely overlooked despite the surge of chart QA research, with clear motivation (disinformation risk).

Comprehensive empirical scope: 19 MLLMs (open and closed, general and chart-specialized) evaluated across multiple existing datasets (CALVI, CHARTOM, VLAT, ChartQA) plus a newly introduced real-world misleading-visualization dataset with manually created MCQs, adding needed real-world grounding beyond synthetic benchmarks.

Two complementary experimental paradigms (MCQ accuracy vs. random baseline/human baseline, and Likert-scale consistency across matched misleading/non-misleading pairs) converge on the same conclusion, strengthening the central claim of vulnerability.

Systematic comparison of six inference-time correction methods with appropriate statistical testing (McNemar's test), and careful attention to the accuracy/non-misleading trade-off, which is explicitly framed as a design criterion rather than ignored.

Extensive supplementary analyses (parametric knowledge confound, table/axes extraction error analysis, misleader-specific breakdowns, DePlot/MatCha comparison, CoT ablation) that provide mechanistic insight into why methods succeed or fail, aiding reproducibility and interpretability.
Code/data release and a full definition table of 17 misleader types improve transparency and reusability for follow-up work.
weaknesses: The misleading/non-misleading datasets are small (n=143/124) with highly imbalanced misleader categories (several with n≤3, e.g., missing data n=1, overplotting n=1, inappropriate pie chart n=1), making per-misleader accuracy claims (Figure 12, Appendix D) statistically fragile despite being discussed as substantive findings.

Correction methods (Experiment 3) are only tested on three mid-sized open-weight MLLMs (Qwen2VL-7B, Ovis1.6-9B, InternVL2.5-8B), all of which start below the random baseline; it is unclear whether findings generalize to top-performing closed models (Claude-3.5-sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-pro) or to smaller/specialized chart models, limiting the generality of the correction-method conclusions.

The abstract's claim that effective methods improve misleading-visualization accuracy "without compromising accuracy on non-misleading ones" is contradicted by the body text, which reports a significant accuracy drop of up to 8.5pp on non-misleading visualizations for table-based QA on two of the three models—this overstatement should be softened.

Redrawing-visualization method depends on code-compilation success and does not support maps; its dependence on chart type being known a priori and on Matplotlib defaults limits real-world applicability, and success/failure is not deeply analyzed beyond compile rates.

Several contemporaneous works (cited: Bendeck & Stasko 2025, Chen et al. 2025, Pandey & Ottley 2025) study closely related MLLM vulnerability to misleading charts, somewhat diminishing the novelty of the core "vulnerability" finding, even though the paper differentiates itself via correction methods and real-world data.

Experiment 1's headline comparisons (accuracy drops, random-baseline comparison) are not accompanied by significance testing or confidence intervals, unlike Experiment 3, creating some inconsistency in rigor across the paper's main claims.

Reliance on a single LLM (Qwen2.5-7B) as the backbone for table-based QA and redrawing means the correction-method comparison partly confounds MLLM table-extraction quality with the downstream reasoning LLM's capability; while DePlot/MatCha are compared in the appendix, this analysis is not integrated into the main results.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: robustness of MLLMs to misleading visualizations, which has clear relevance to disinformation and AI safety in NLP/vision-language research.

Comprehensive empirical scope: 19 MLLMs (open-weight and commercial, including chart-specialized models) evaluated across multiple existing benchmarks (CALVI, CHARTOM, VLAT, ChartQA) plus a newly introduced real-world misleading-visualization dataset with manually created MCQs.

Three complementary experiments (QA accuracy, Likert-scale consistency, and correction methods) provide converging evidence for the central claim that MLLMs are vulnerable to misleaders, with appropriate statistical testing (McNemar's test, paired t-test).

Thorough analysis beyond top-line numbers: breakdown by misleader type, comparison to human accuracy from prior literature, investigation of parametric-knowledge effects on real-world data, and extensive manual error analysis of intermediate table/axes extraction (Appendices C, D, G–I) that helps explain why particular correction methods succeed or fail.
Reasonably reproducible: fixed decoding (temperature 0), documented prompts (Appendix B), and stated intent to release code and data.

Honest reporting of negative results (four of six correction methods ineffective) and of trade-offs (table-based QA hurting non-misleading accuracy), which strengthens the credibility of the study rather than overselling results.
Clear positioning relative to concurrent/parallel work, explaining the distinct contribution (real-world visualizations, correction-method trade-off analysis).
weaknesses: The misleading-visualization datasets remain small (n=143) and unevenly distributed across 17 misleader categories (e.g., several categories have only 1 instance), which limits the statistical reliability of per-misleader accuracy claims (e.g., 0% or 100% accuracy figures based on very few examples).

The proposed correction methods (table-based QA, redrawing, warnings) are largely adaptations of existing techniques (Liu et al. 2023a,b; Fan et al. 2022) rather than novel methodological contributions; the paper's contribution is primarily an evaluation/benchmarking study rather than a new technique.

Human-accuracy comparisons are drawn from different studies with different question sets and subject pools (CALVI, CHARTOM), so the human-vs-MLLM comparison, while suggestive, is not a fully controlled comparison.

The two effective correction methods still depend heavily on an error-prone intermediate table/code-generation extraction step performed by an LLM, meaning the fixes are somewhat brittle and their generalization to other MLLMs/LLMs (only one LLM, Qwen2.5-7B, used for extraction) is unverified.

The study is restricted to inference-time, prompting-based interventions; no exploration of fine-tuning or training-based mitigation, which could be a more durable solution and is only briefly mentioned as future work.
Some claims (e.g., "first comprehensive study," "first analysis of six correction methods") slightly overstate novelty given closely related concurrent work already cited in the related-work section.

The consistency experiment (Experiment 2) uses only four visualization pairs, which is a very small sample for drawing conclusions about model consistency, even though it is presented as corroborating the accuracy findings.
